summary: A rich man's manager, accused of wasting property, acts decisively before dismissal by reducing client debts and creating a network of welcome. The master praises his shrewdness, not his dishonesty; Jesus presses disciples to convert ‘unrighteous Mammon’ into faithful relationships, because money reveals loyalty and cannot share mastery with God. Pharisees described as lovers of money ridicule him; Jesus answers that God knows hearts, then places kingdom proclamation beside the enduring law and a compressed divorce warning. A second rich man dresses and feasts splendidly while poor Lazarus lies at his gate. Death reverses their positions. In Hades, the rich man still treats Lazarus as an errand-runner, but Abraham says the living already have Moses and the prophets; even resurrection will not persuade people who refuse to hear them.
whyItMatters: Luke treats possessions as a spiritual power with public consequences. Shrewdness is redirected toward mercy, and the unnamed rich man's damnation is narrated not for having purple fabric but for making a suffering neighbor invisible at his own gate. In the story, Abraham holds that Moses and the prophets already say enough to act.

context.author: The anonymous author, traditionally identified as Luke, pairing two difficult wealth stories with sayings about loyalty, law, and judgment
context.audience: Theophilus and a wider Greek-reading audience; the chapter addresses property, debt, patronage, Torah, and care for the poor
context.date: Commonly dated around AD 80–90, after AD 70; earlier dates in the 60s and later ones into the early second century are defended; part of the journey discourse
context.setting: Imagined estate accounts, public dispute, and an after-death reversal framed by Abraham
context.literaryForm: Provocative manager parable, interpretive sayings, controversy, compressed legal saying, and named exemplary tale

outline.heading: Manager accused and acting before dismissal
outline.note: Facing dismissal, a manager tells one debtor to write fifty for a hundred batos of oil, another eighty; the lord commends him

outline.heading: Mammon, faithful stewardship, and two masters
outline.note: He says the one faithful in little is faithful in much, and that no servant can serve two masters, 'God and Mammon'.

outline.heading: Money-loving ridicule, heart, kingdom, law, and divorce
outline.note: Scoffing Pharisees are told God knows their hearts; the law and prophets were until John; whoever divorces and marries another commits adultery

outline.heading: Rich man and Lazarus in life and death
outline.note: Beggar Lazarus lies sore-covered at a rich man's gate; both die, and Abraham tells the rich man in Hades a great gulf is fixed

outline.heading: Moses, prophets, and refusal beyond a resurrection sign
outline.note: He asks that Lazarus go to his brothers; Abraham says 'They have Moses and the prophets'; one rising from the dead would not persuade

keyVerses.text: I tell you, make for yourselves friends by means of unrighteous mammon, so that when you fail, they may receive you into the eternal tents.
keyVerses.why: Possessions are redirected from mastery and insulation toward merciful relationships with eternal weight.

keyVerses.text: No servant can serve two masters, for either he will hate the one and love the other; or else he will hold to one and despise the other. You aren’t able to serve God and Mammon.”
keyVerses.why: The chapter personifies wealth as a rival claimant to service, not a neutral quantity.

keyVerses.text: “He said to him, ‘If they don’t listen to Moses and the prophets, neither will they be persuaded if one rises from the dead.’”
keyVerses.why: Failure to practice Scripture cannot be cured merely by demanding a more spectacular sign.

questions.question: Why is a dishonest manager praised?
questions.answer: The master praises phronimōs — prudent or wise action — not the earlier waste or possible fraud. Facing a closed future, the manager uses present authority to create people who will receive him. Jesus extracts urgency and foresight from a morally compromised character, as parables sometimes do, without endorsing every deed.

questions.question: What exactly did the debt reductions do?
questions.answer: They cut the bills, oil from a hundred batos to fifty and wheat from a hundred cors to eighty; the story does not say whose loss this was. The manager's stated aim is that the debtors ‘may receive me into their houses’ (16:4). The interpretive sayings shift attention from reconstructing the ledger to using wealth faithfully.

questions.question: What is ‘unrighteous Mammon’?
questions.answer: Mamōnas is a Semitic term for wealth or property, personified here as a master. On one common reading, ‘unrighteous’ reflects money's entanglement with unequal systems and its power to deceive, not a claim that every coin is stolen. Disciples must handle it as another's entrusted resource, never as the source of identity or security.

questions.question: Does giving money earn entrance into heaven?
questions.answer: The text does not describe purchasing salvation. It says wealth can be used to create friends and reveals whether someone is faithful with what is temporary and belongs to another. In Luke, generosity embodies repentance and received mercy; it does not put God in the recipient's debt.

questions.question: Why does Luke suddenly mention law and divorce?
questions.answer: The sayings answer people who justify themselves while ridiculing Jesus's money teaching. Kingdom proclamation does not dissolve Torah's moral seriousness; the divorce line supplies a concrete case where socially respectable self-justification can conceal harm. Its compression requires comparison with fuller teachings before forming pastoral policy.

questions.question: Is the rich man condemned simply for being rich?
questions.answer: The story emphasizes conspicuous luxury beside Lazarus's visible hunger and wounds at his gate. The man is not accused of one dramatic crime; his daily indifference is the indictment. Even after death he asks Abraham to send Lazarus as a servant, showing that his hierarchy remains unchanged.

questions.question: Is this a literal map of the afterlife?
questions.answer: Jesus uses familiar reversal imagery — Hades, Abraham's bosom, flame, and a fixed chasm — to expose present wealth and ignored Scripture. The story carries claims about judgment and irreversible consequence, but on one common reading, building a complete geography from each narrative detail mistakes parable-like rhetoric for a travel diagram.

questions.question: Why is Lazarus named when the rich man is not?
questions.answer: Lazaros is apparently a Greek form of Eleazar, ‘whom God helps.’ The person invisible at the gate is given a name, while the socially famous man becomes anonymous. Luke reverses whose identity heaven remembers; the name does not make this Lazarus the man in John 11.

glossary.def: Semitic term for wealth or property, personified as a rival master.

Image of honored closeness to Abraham (16:22-23).
Greek term for the realm of the dead; not identical in every context with Gehenna or later popular hell imagery.
